extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, and journal staff responsible for submission and peer-review workflows (particularly in health/medical journals)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical workflows for journals to adopt, endorse, or require reporting guidelines so submitted manuscripts contain the minimum information needed for understanding, replication, and inclusion in systematic reviews. Addresses common editor/publisher concerns and offers low-burden implementation options, tools, and templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines define the minimum set of information needed for a particular kind of study so manuscripts can be understood, evaluated, replicated, and included in systematic reviews and clinical decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups of clinicians, academics, systematic reviewers, and statisticians have defined these minimum items. Guidelines exist for most general study types and for specific outcomes/methods that are often reported badly. Without these items, work may be unusable and wasted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use guidelines during writing and study design, not only at submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines should be used while writing an article (and ideally at the research design phase), rather than treated as a box-checking exercise only at submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educate authors so they integrate use into writing and design; the toolkit includes a template author letter requesting resubmission once made compliant and explaining why guidelines are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require a submitted checklist with page numbers as a completeness review
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals require authors to submit a checklist indicating the page number on which each guideline item has been addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice is not merely administrative: it helps authors report every necessary item by acting as a 'completeness review'. The toolkit provides editable versions of common checklists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endorse vs require implementation routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals can choose a simple 'endorse' route or a stricter 'require checklist' route to implement reporting guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'endorse' route may only require a change to 'Instructions to Authors' and links to guidelines (low burden). The 'require checklist' route involves mandatory checklist submission and may include editorial checks at triage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial administrative staff can check guideline compliance at triage
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals can train editorial/admin staff to check guideline compliance as part of initial submission triage rather than relying solely on peer reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach reduces burden on peer reviewers and can be integrated into submission triage; EQUATOR toolkit includes training resources and template letters for returning manuscripts for resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peer reviewers as a compliance triage tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers can be asked to check guideline compliance (for example, ask a first reviewer to check compliance before recruiting subsequent reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a manuscript fails the compliance check, peer review can halt and the article is returned; the toolkit includes template instructions for reviewers and editable checklists with additional explanation for reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endorsement of reporting guidelines improves reporting quality
rubrics_metrics.description: There is evidence that journals endorsing reporting guidelines see a significant increase in reporting quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page asserts a 'significant increase' in reporting quality when journals endorse guidelines, supporting their adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer and editorial review alone are insufficient to ensure complete reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing peer and editorial review frequently miss essential reporting items; every specialty and study type checked suffers from poor reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting guidelines are a helpful tool for reviewers to systematically check that essential information has been reported; they complement traditional review rather than replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementing guidelines generally speeds up publication workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing reporting guidelines speeds up publication of well-reported articles and accelerates rejection of poorly reported articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: authors have a clear template when writing; editors can triage and return poorly reported manuscripts in minutes rather than sending them to lengthy peer review; peer reviewers can triage faster and spend less time on articles needing major rewriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerns about delaying publication are mitigated by faster triage and clearer author guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: While writing may take longer if authors hadn't previously considered all checklist items, catching those issues early avoids wasted peer reviewer time and can shorten overall time to publication for well-reported manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer author writing time may indicate methodological flaws that should be addressed; it's better to identify these before peer review than after.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting guidelines do not make articles formulaic or restrict creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines mandate the minimum information to be reported (mainly methods and results) but do not prescribe language or the content/style of introduction, discussion, or interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A creatively written article that lacks essential information is not useful science; guidelines protect scientific usability without dictating narrative style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-cost implementation options are available
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals concerned about cost can adopt low-burden options (e.g., 'endorse' route) without significant resource investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EQUATOR toolkit provides workflows, templates, and links so journals can start with a simple endorsement that changes only the Instructions to Authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good reporting is a shared responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility for complete, transparent reporting is shared among authors, reviewers, editors, and journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes that good reporting 'is everyone’s responsibility' and that journals play a facilitating role by implementing guidelines and tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors may find guidelines onerous initially but benefit from clearer templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines offer authors a clear template that reduces uncertainty about what to report; initial extra time may be required if items were not considered at design/writing stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This upfront effort can reveal methodological issues that are better corrected before peer review than after, and ultimately reduces wasted reviewer/editor effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical tools, templates, and training are provided to support implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: The toolkit includes a workflow for endorsement, template author letters for resubmission, template instructions for peer reviewers, editable checklists, and training resources for editorial staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These materials are intended to lower the barrier to adopting either the endorse or require-checklist routes and to standardize implementation across journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting guidelines by study type (resource list)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of major reporting guidelines for main study types is provided: Randomised trials (CONSORT + Extensions), Observational studies (STROBE + Extensions), Systematic reviews (PRISMA + Extensions), Study protocols (SPIRIT, PRISMA-P), Diagnostic/prognostic studies (STARD, TRIPOD), Case reports (CARE + Extensions), Clinical practice guidelines (AGREE, RIGHT), Qualitative research (SRQR, COREQ), Animal pre-clinical studies (ARRIVE), Quality improvement studies (SQUIRE + Extensions), Economic evaluations (CHEERS + Extensions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These named guidelines are the canonical standards journals can link to or require; the toolkit groups them by study type to help editors select appropriate guidance for incoming manuscripts.
